rows.label: Marginal cost of public funds: what a dollar of tax revenue costs those who pay, in dollars

source.title: US Office of Management and Budget, Circular A-94: Guidelines and Discount Rates for Benefit-Cost Analysis of Federal Programs
source.page: section 11, Special Guidance for Public Investment Analysis
source.quote: Recent studies of the U.S. tax system suggest a range of values for the marginal excess burden, of which a reasonable estimate is 25 cents per dollar of revenue.

rows.explainer: Raising a dollar of tax costs the economy more than a dollar, through the work and spending it discourages. OMB's benefit-cost guidance takes 25 cents per dollar of revenue for US taxes, so 1.25. Range 1 (money shifted from other spending, not new taxes) to 1.5, the top of the published estimates for rich countries' taxes (Dahlby 2008, The Marginal Cost of Public Funds, MIT Press: about 1.1 to 1.5) and above most estimates for low- and middle-income countries' taxes (Auriol and Warlters 2012, Journal of Development Economics, 38 African countries: mostly 1.1 to 1.3). Read by every model that values government money its advocacy wins net of what it costs those who pay.

rows.label: How US federal taxes fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log-income scale a dollar taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption; a tax proportional to consumption costs 1 over the national-accounts mean (a multiple of 1), a progressive one less (above 1). Federal programmes are paid for by the federal income tax and borrowing, which fall mostly on richer households: 1.4, range 1 (borrowing repaid by everyone alike) to 2. Read by every model that values federal money net of what it costs those who pay; state and local money (regressive sales taxes) takes its own figure.
